blocks.x: All right, we're started. What's today's date? First of August, 1970 and 8. 1970 and where are we? We are still, since this is a continuation, at 4140 Sena Drive, Las Cruces, New Mexico, zip code 88001. S-I-N-N-E-R? S-S-E-N-N-A. Okay. I never thought about that before. Sent a laxative, as a matter of fact. Spelled the same way? Same plan. Oh, this is named after a poem. Yeah. All these streets along here are named after a poem. On Mission Bell, yeah. Well, that's a new street in a different subdivision. I see. Yeah. Okay. Now, I'm just curious about it. Oh, and your name. Bernard Steino. I've got three names on here now, and you're Dick Al. Yeah, Dick Al. Or do you go as Richard B. Or Arbinian? Anyway. I go all the different kind of ways. Anyway. You want to get back to... No, I just encourage it. Was your mother named Mayer, right? Mayer, M-A-Y-A-R. Yeah, I'm just curious. And that's where you got the Mayer in the middle. Yeah. Yeah. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
Okay, the lead has gone through.

New Orleans Item was doing an expose on gambling, and there was a poker game going on in the back room of the place. And one of the habitués spotted my camera in flash and had this great plan that would give everybody a laugh where I would go in and take a flash picture or perhaps just pretend to take a flash picture of the card game, and I managed in a fairly friendly manner to decline, but I got nervous every time I walked by the card room to go to the John after that.
Facing the band, the John was to the left.
As I remember, yeah.
Yeah, they had the entrance right there.
Yeah.
Anyway, was there much gambling going on in the dance halls? I'm trying to think of some that I noticed.
This wasn't a dance hall, actually. It was a neighborhood bar, and I don't really, if there was room for dancing, it was minimal.
Yeah.

But the band was there, so I suspect there was a little bit, but it wasn't a terribly big place. I didn't, in the neighborhood places, I didn't see much gambling, but I suspect there may have been some if people felt like it. Gambling, private games at any rate, were pretty ubiquitous, certainly at the time. There was a lot of public gambling going on, too. I was never quite sure why the item was so busy with it, because both the gambling houses in Jefferson and St. Bernard Parish were running wide open at the time, and did for some years thereafter.
I remember these places as maybe being neighborhood bars, but neighborhood bars with dancing. Like Lutton's had a bar in front.
Right, and a medium-sized sort of a hall with some tables in it behind.
Yeah.
And there are still places like this in New Orleans, as you know. Yeah.
And it didn't seem to me to be too much trouble to convert into a dance hall in a hurry.

No, it wouldn't have been. You know, the inside was fairly, was pretty much square or rectangular and didn't have much built in around. Some of them had pretty good acoustics, some of them didn't. I think the main thing people wanted was for the bands to play fairly loud, and that was fun. We went to some places, to similar neighborhood places in Algiers and Marrero, pretty much the same sort of picture. Different bands, usually, most of them didn't have a regular sort of a dancing arrangement that I know of.
What about the kitty in those places?

Well, most places had a cigar box or a milk bottle or a can, I think quite frequently supplied by the band, sometimes marked kitty, sometimes just discreetly displayed on top of the piano or in front, and sometimes with a sign saying feed the kitty. And people tended to fairly regularly. I remember one particularly enjoyable occasion, which I think I got invited to kind of late and wound up, I believe, only Greenwood and I went. But the manager of the George Lewis band at the time was a fellow, an attorney named Nick Gagliano. Nick, I had met following bands around, and I think also at the New Orleans Jazz Club meetings, and he was a nice kind of a guy. And when I went to medical school, which I started a little after I met Nick, this was in fall, I started in fall of 48, I found out that one of my classmates was also named Nick Gagliano, and this was a cousin of the attorney, and one of the faculty people, the ancillary faculty, was also Gagliano, and I think he was Nick too. And they were all related. And somewhere along the line, I think probably in 49 or 50, conceivably 51, one of the Knicks, and I think the attorneys, parents had their 25th wedding anniversary, and they rented, this was on a Sunday, they rented a large club in Jefferson Parish off the airline highway, and invited all the family, and they also invited me, and I think Greenwood.
And me, I went to...
Were you at that?
Yeah.
Great, I didn't remember.
Yeah, I was at some,
either at our wedding reception,
some such thing like that, I remember very...

And it was very exciting. Oh, it was a great party. It was a great big place. There were all sorts of people there, ranging from newborn to in their 80s, I suspect. Mostly kinfolk of the Gaglianos. But one of the girls in the family was an exotic or semi-exotic dancer of some sort, so she chimied or something of the sort at one point. There were great tubs of beer and food and all sorts of things, and the band played for hours and hours. Finally got away late in the evening. They were scheduled to do a broadcast. I forget which station, and I remember watching or helping, I forget which, I suspect just watching, slow drag, Paul Vigio, I think tie his base to the top of an automobile so he could transport it. Lovely party, really had a ball.
George was broadcasting it on WTPS at Lee Circle at one point, but I don't know, I seem to think that was Sunday afternoon or something.
This was late. This was, I think they were supposed to be there around 6.30 or 7 or something like that, so it probably wasn't that particular,
sponsored by Jack Spears,

I remember. That was a great party. And there were other parties and dances and things that any number of people gave in New Orleans, organizations and the like that had bands, and they were fun. Music was often good. Musicians played pretty much what they wanted with some request. Yeah.
At the dance halls when they fed the kitty, it would usually be for their request, if I remember that. Yeah.
Basically speaking, if you wanted the band to play something, somebody would go up and say, do you... .
We've got reel two on there, August the 1st, 1978. Bernie, you were talking about going in with a band?

Oh yeah, as I was saying on the end of the other tape, you did it a lot more than I did, but basically everyone seemed to accept and welcome you if you went in with the band, and I don't remember ever having been hassled at this.
No, not at all. At times I was hassled, visiting the musicians backstage on Bourbon Street.
By club owners and the like?
Yeah, backstage is not the word, the back room. Well, the police station's in the police station. Didn't want you going around talking and interfering with the musicians.
Hmm.

Well, and sometimes even at Lutchen's I'd be talking to Ernest Rogers or somebody like that, the drummer, and one of the Lutchen brothers would give me a hard time. Hmm. Which is why I was always bothering the musicians. Of course they were rather pugnacious, both of the brothers having been boxers, I think. Oh.
Well, that's something I didn't know anything about. Yeah.

Well, shall we start up with a new subject now? Yeah. You can't think of any place you came in where you snuck in with the musicians. Uh, what were some of the brass bands that you heard, that you remember the names? How many?

Oh, I didn't really hear that many. I heard the Eureka, the Young Tuxedo, a couple of times. And there were some that I ran across that didn't have any identification that I knew of. And I wasn't sure whether these were regularly constituted organizations or just pickup groups.
I remember George Williams' brass band as being around, but I don't remember any, uh, anything, any photographs you made.
I don't either. I know I went by the identification, you know, I went by the identification on the drums, and it was about as far as I knew. Yeah.
Well, sometimes we knew individual people. Yeah. But not everybody in those bands. I would ask, and I think I made a lot of notes in too.
Yeah, you were doing that. I knew, actually, one of the ways that I knew about parades more often than not was by, uh, Washington, George. Which Washington was that? Snare drum with the Eureka.
Edmund.
Edmund?
And his nickname was Sun White.

Uh, who, uh, worked at the medical school and knew that I liked, that I liked to follow the bands, and he would usually tell me if they were going to play. Which I always appreciated. And he also played with George Williams too. Oh, did he?
He, do you remember he once said trambone to you?
No.
We talked about that. Well, you told me about it.
I, I may have.
Speculating as to why anyone would say trambone.
Well, you know, that wasn't the first time I heard that usage.
Yeah.
And I wasn't sure whether the earlier usage, which was by, oh, sometimes sort of affected, uh, Dixieland types.
Mm-hmm.
Was artificial or, or a legitimate sort of usage.
What do you mean by Dixieland?

Uh, basically, uh, white musicians, particularly white, non-New Orleans jazz musicians, playing, I guess, in the, in the white New Orleans style from the, from the twenties. Did you make a big distinction between white and black musicians then? Uh, generally speaking, I liked the way the black musicians played.
Mm-hmm.

But, uh, it depended a lot. For example, I very much liked some of the so-called jazz revival white bands. And I, in fact, the first band that ever, that I ever listened to, uh, in person. And that really excited me was Lou Waters' jazz band. Well, the Yerba Buena Jazz Band, which I caught in San Francisco in, I think, late November of 1945. No, no, it was late November of 1946, at the, uh, Dawn Club off of Market, about a block. And, uh, I was on my way back home to New Orleans after having been processed out of the Army in Seattle. And, uh, stopped over for a day or two to visit an old friend of my family's. And, uh, saw this ad in the paper about the Yerba Buena Jazz Band, which I had heard vaguely of one place or another. And I went down to the Dawn Club and really, really got excited. Again, the first live band that I'd, that I'd heard without, with any idea what I heard, they played a number of sets of four, five, or six tunes. Uh, I don't think they played any, any of them twice. Uh, they, uh, they had a program with each tune list, with each set, and each tune in each set listed. And they must have played, oh, I would guess, at least eight or ten sets during the evening and played all sorts of things. Uh, mostly traditional, a wide range of things. Uh, they, they had, as I remember, uh, two trumpets and a Turk Murphy on trombone. Uh, I think Bob Helm was on clarinet then. Uh, I think I've got a program somewhere around from it. I may have, I may have given it to the archives. And I, I think I did, from that particular time. Uh, one of the things that amused me and interested me was they had a small menu besides drinks. And they had red beans and rice with grated cheese. And some San Francisco-style French bread. And it was the first time I'd ever encountered the idea of having grated Italian-style cheese on red beans and rice. I don't think I ever saw it anywhere else either. It was pretty good, though. And I hadn't had dinner, and that was a, that was a, a charming idea. But I listened to a great number of things. And there, there were some tunes I heard that night that I've never heard since, I think. And one, at least, of which I remembered many of the lyrics to, uh, which was Mrs. Skinner's Chicken Dinner. Uh, but it, it was an exciting sort of an experience. But that style I never considered Dixieland. Uh, Dixieland I considered more. But, of course, the, the, the, the Urba Buena Band style and the Turk Murphy Band style later, was, uh, primarily based on black bands of the twenties and earlier and perhaps a bit later.

Were there many people who liked to go listen to black bands and collect the different things? Collected their records, uh? Not, not in New Orleans. I don't know that there ever have been in New Orleans. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. We were, around the New Orleans Record Shop, we'd see the people. Certainly. Who'd come in and buy the records. And I'm, I'm trying to think of who I saw that came in there.
And, I, I, I used to wonder how the shop managed to exist, considering the fact that it never seemed awfully busy.
Only with people who liked to talk and listen, not buy.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Looked like it was one of these unintentional non-profit organizations. Mm-hmm. Yeah.

Yeah, but, uh, well my feeling was that we were somewhat considered outcasts, and I would, uh, I can remember going to a meeting of people who collected records, supposedly, and really liked them, and one of the leading lights said, Joyce Lewis and Paul Barberin don't play jazz, they play Creole music, which I found a bit weird. But, uh, you know, you're full of people, the world is full of people like that.
Yeah. Who was that?

Oh, I can't. We'll have to restrict this. His name was Pete Miller. You know, a perfectly nice man with a lot of record, but he just didn't consider that style jazz. I imagine that Sharky was jazz to him and anything like that, you know, but, but just to him, any black bands didn't play jazz.

Well, there were, you know, there were people like this. You did have, you did have, uh, Nick LaRocca claiming that he invented jazz, as other people have claimed before and since. And, uh, I suspect if you take the right rationalization, you can come up with it. You've got a, you've got a great story, maybe this isn't the place for it, about, uh, the people up on the bayou who invented jazz. That ought to be put down sometime. I don't even remember that. That's, you know, when you and Fred Ramsey were, were up around Napoleonville. Oh yeah. Or somewhere up there.
Yeah, well, I thought they were all kind of claimed like that. I've forgotten what they said.
Well, you know, they said they started, they started improvising and stuff. Oh yeah, another one you're talking about now. Yeah.

Yeah, how they'd stopped reading and began to improvise. And I finally asked them what year, and it was in the thirties I didn't believe. Yeah. Made it very exciting. Well, I mean, so much research is done on, on bands and nobody ever stops to ask them what style they were playing. And, uh, only recently I was talking to Kid Sheik, who really liked Barrel House trumpet players and was one himself, but he liked people like Chris Kelly, and, uh, Joey Dim in particular, Wooden Joe Nicholas. And, uh, anyhow, uh, I asked him what he thought about Manuel Perez. I'd never been able to figure out what Manuel Perez I like at all. I asked him if he could play by ear at all, and he said, oh yes, he was the best of those reading trumpet players for playing anything like jazz, for really getting away from it. But, I mean, there's so many different viewpoints, and words are used so trickily. Yeah. I mean, and people used to say musician, and he's a musician, and, uh, they met a reader, if you remember. No, that I didn't know.
I just thought it was an archaic term that was sort of charming, but didn't know what it would signify. And, uh, it's almost as though you didn't have to play, as long as you could read it.

You were marvelous then. I mean, it went to that extreme with some people. Yeah. I'm sure it depended on who said it. Yes, and people. Well, I can remember playing with the music, and I was like, I'm sure it was a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of a little bit of colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless to colorless distorted the people we thought of as being Jim Crow. It certainly influenced me so that I, well, I sometimes would not bother to go listen to white bands that I later learned to enjoy, even though I always was arguing with people to listen to both, and I'd make, I can remember making record collectors sit down and listen to Johnny Byerstoffer's band after they said that only the Black Rans could play.
I'll tell you, that was, Byerstoffer was, I think they only got about four sides out of, two sides? Two. And I still think those were two of the best sides out of New Orleans in the 20s that I'd
ever run across. I always regretted that I never interviewed him, I knew him. Was he? Oh. And he came back, do you remember? No, I don't. He even played at the famous store for a little while.
And nobody, huh, too bad nobody recorded him. Somebody should.
Well, there were tapes of him then, later on. But he, you know, he's gone through the process, having played in big bands and changed his style and everything.

Well, I know one of the things that really intrigued me, I don't remember we've talked about this book. No, I don't think so. Well, anyway, what really intrigued me was some of the, how some of the bands that I'd consider to be local more or less hack-type bands really could play,
and sometimes did play exceptional jazz. Oh yeah, I've enjoyed Shockey more sometimes than others. So I just thought it was terrific when he was really playing.
Well you know, you listen to his old, to his records from the 30s, and some of them are extremely good. Oh, the 20s, yeah. But I mean this is in the 50s. Yeah, I know that.

I'm talking about when I would really enjoy him sometimes when he, well, I think every musician can can get in a rut, black or white, if he's playing on Bourbon Street especially, because I feel the pressure is on them there to be in a rut.
Well, I think musicians are, or jazz musicians are really in a difficult sort of a bind.
Mm-hmm.

If they're playing to suit jazz enthusiasts, then they are expected, or expect themselves to live up to certain things that they, that they want. If they're playing for the general public, they've got to play from a totally different bias. I'm not sure that, that you ever quite know what they want.

Well I always felt, and based on a lot of years of observing people, that when the jazz musicians got a chance to play without restrictions, that the public liked it, whereas when some nightclub owner, some smart money guy is telling them what to play, then usually the thing falls flat, and the public can tell the difference. Now that's, goes against maybe what the critics say, but it's very easy to sit around and be a critic. It's quite different from sitting there and observing what actually goes on. I mean, it's very easy to theorize about things if you're sitting there listening to a lot of records. It's one thing to go through the ratings on radio programs, and and to watch audiences and watch people have a good time of why they're doing what they do, and just observe it. Of course, and again, one thing I think that it is, it's very hard to separate out

your own feelings. You don't think it can be done. You do the best you can, but you're stuck with some of it. Yeah, but you can sure tell something for motor reaction, if nothing else. Yeah, you can tell, yeah, you certainly can tell a lot. You just can't separate it out too precisely.

Yeah. The applause, things like that. Well, and I've heard, gone to listen to Archibald a lot, he used to play just off, wherever you know St. Peter the piano player, the guy who made Stackely, I don't know if he was playing around when you were. I don't know. I know the name, but I don't know why. Anyway, he played solo piano a lot. I'd go and listen to him. When the crowd was right, the barmaid would say, well how come you don't play like this for us? Well I mean it does make a difference when people appreciate your music certainly. Although you know, I might as well

say this since it gives me a chance to, and it's something you and I have moaned about for years. Really, it really irritates me to an extreme when you get an audience that applauds after every solo. Yeah. Well, it messes the next soloist up. It sure does. Or it would seem to me it would. Yeah. Never heard a musician comment on this. No. But from the standpoint of people who are really

listening. Yeah. And they want to hear the thing. And of course, one thing about the type of music that we used to enjoy so much and hear live under those circumstances was that the musicians had a sense of form and they saw how the thing was going to develop. And you knew that from the fact that they would begin with an introduction, for example. Yeah. And so that the whole thing was a

building process. You know what? It was this climax. Excuse me. You know one of the things that maybe was a difference at one time between white musicians, Dixieland musicians, and the black bands was that to some extent many of the Dixieland bands had a sort of routine format of one solo after another. And the black bands more frequently played together with some solos and some ensembles. This, I think, changed with time. And I think the black bands imitated the white bands, which I think, well, I thought it was a mistake.

Which leads me to a question I wanted to ask you. Do you remember any musicians that seemed particularly lazy to you? Lazy? Yeah. Hmm. I mean, obviously some of these people have been working one or two jobs in addition to
what they did at night. Not often. Yeah. It's not something I particularly thought about in connection with them. So I really, you know, my answer doesn't make, wouldn't make much sense. Well,

if you're sitting around playing a job, and of course the nightclub owners wanted them to take long breaks between maybe a couple of them. They'd play two tunes and then take a long break so that people could drink. That's what was the theory of legends, why they took such frequent long breaks. The set would consist of two tunes, then a break, and then two tunes, and then a break. Well, anyway, if you have, say, a seven piece band, and you have seven soloists, it seems to me that the trumpet player and the clarinet player and the trombonist could get pretty lazy. And they just want to rest. The rest of most of the music. Yeah, they could. Huh. No, it's not something I noticed particularly, though.

Did you notice any enthusiasm? I noticed enthusiasm principally in a band that either played a night or two a week or had fairly recently gotten a full, gotten a five or six-night-a-week job. My basic recollection is that a band that played regularly quite frequently got stale and fast. They might have a good night from time to time, or even a few good numbers, but basically they didn't get terribly enthusiastic, which I attributed to, oh, perhaps boredom. It was, you know, we used to talk about this sometimes, that maybe the band that played a lot of people. Maybe these guys did better if they didn't play full-time.
Yeah. What about, uh, do you remember any fancy drill at the parades?

Not from the musicians particularly. No, no, I mean the- Oh, the marching groups? The, uh, the social organizations. Oh, yeah. There were, uh, in fact some of the photographs show, in particular show, and as I remember this was a young men's Olympians organization, I think. Yeah. That had both, that had sort of a paramilitary unit, uh, and I think a ladies auxiliary. I'm not sure, so sure about the ladies auxiliary with the Olympians. It may have been, it may have been an odd fellows group.
Yeah, well, they have the household of Ruth, I think, the odd fellows.

But, uh, the, uh, the young men of the Olympians, uh, had a, had a khaki, uh, uniform. Uh-huh. With, uh, a certain, with the officer types carrying sabers. And, uh, uh, although basically they didn't do anything very fancy. As I remember the odd fellows had, had a men's unit which did some fairly elaborate, medium elaborate military type drill. And a ladies organization, the ladies dressed, as I recall, in white two-piece uniforms with a, with a, uh, uh, barracks type cap, I think you'd call it. A build cap.
Uh-huh.
And, uh, would do similar sorts of drills. And they, they looked very smart. They were in the photographs, yeah. Yeah, they were both of those drills.
The drill teams, I can remember messing up a lot. They just get confused.
Drill teams do if you don't, if they don't practice pretty constantly.
Yeah, well, it's easy to mess the difference between left and right.
Yeah.
As you and I know, from years of experience, like everybody else. Uh, what about the stops? Your photographs show them coming into the rest stops. The, uh, the clubs.
Uh, clubs and sometimes private homes where...
I mean the marching, the social aid and pleasure clubs and the... Oh, oh, oh. And the, uh, societies, but none of them.

Yeah, they, these groups, the parade tended to stop at, oh, pretty regular intervals. Frequently at a bar or a bar and grocery combination place. Mm-hmm. Sometimes at private homes. Mm-hmm. And basically they would turn in more or less in military fashion, usually in the single file, uh, flanking movement. And the band would circle together on the sidewalk, as a rule, or just out in the street. Mm-hmm. And play while the group went inside. And then the band and the second line would relax outside while the members of the organization would relax inside. And then after a while they'd come out and get, get back to it again. Yeah, I even got invited in a few times. Did you?

I can remember Herman Sherman telling me how to, well, we would get sandwiches that were wrapped up in wax paper, as I remember it. And he'd show me how to slip them down in my umbrella. I'd have this umbrella which was, so you'd have plenty of sandwiches. Well, I mean, umbrellas were very useful things. I never thought of that purpose. No. It's just one of those little things that just came back to it.
Obviously, obviously you can't roll your brawly very tightly if you're carrying sandwiches. No, it was very loose, in fact.
And umbrellas were nice for rain and sunshine. Dancing purposes.
Mm-hmm.

Let's see, we talked about the Grand Marshals, and you talked about the Eureka recording session. Yeah, I have a feeling about that. Uh, did you, we were talking about social classes, and you know, really nice people didn't do this, and so forth. And so forth, and... I guess there were some nice people who even listened to jazz, but it had to be the right band. I think, too. I think that was fun.

Well, I suspect that there were some nice people who thought for themselves and did not... Mm-hmm. ...didn't feel as encumbered as other people did. I suspect Aksushan probably was one of them, despite some of our annoyances with him.
Yeah.
And I remember, I suspect maybe his father, in a sense, may not have been. I remember seeing a couple of his paintings in Harry's office.
Mm-hmm.

And being impressed with the, both with the paintings and with the non-conventional technique that he used in them. I'm sure, you know, there've all, there always have been people who didn't necessarily believe everything their parents told them. Well, I didn't, yeah, I didn't think that, uh,
Ed Maugham was one of those. I think he liked Barrel House music.
Mm-hmm.

And of course, there were a certain number of people who snuck off to the Red Light District to listen to piano players. And they would relate this to me. They didn't seem particularly ashamed of it, and sang it even in mixed company then.

Of course, you also got people with some other attitudes. I remember, you remember this book of, this book of Belok's pictures that, that Lee Friedlander did with the... Yeah. ...extensive and partially imaginary, or at least reconstructed, uh, conversation in it with Johnny Wiggs talking about the, about the wallpaper from, uh, Mahogany Hall, and how he had to, how he felt he had to disinfect it in a way.

Well, he talked specifically to us at length about that in the record shop, I think. And Greenwood and I were laughing, you know, and I, I don't remember what it said in the interview now. I've got the, you know, the typescript of the interview even, yeah. Well, he got the book almost at hand. But I don't remember that he got that specific, but he...

He got pretty specific. Well, he didn't think it was too clean, anyhow. Yeah, you know, and this was, this was wallpaper that had been on the wall of a building that had been unoccupied for at least 20 or 30 years. Yeah. And, incidentally, well, you, you remember Greenwood and I, uh, got quantities of that wallpaper too. And I think, I don't know, Johnny, I don't know if Johnny heard about it from us or, or from whom.
I think he went with us one day.
I have.
Or maybe he had.
No, I just, I, no, somebody came in with some, uh, some kind of artifacts made, made out of ballast. Mm-hm.
The guy who came in I think was Thurman Reeves who had that, well he had a doorknob and you could peep through the keyhole, you remember? And then he had the newel post.
Yeah, something like that. But Greenwood and I went over and there wasn't an awful lot to rip off except wallpaper and a couple of panes of fancy bathroom glass.

segments.title: Recording opening: date, address and name spellings
segments.summary: Tape starts on 1 August 1978 at the interviewee's Las Cruces home; they sort out spellings of his name and street and the interviewer's name.

segments.title: Photographing near a poker game in a neighborhood bar
segments.summary: A habitue wanted him to fake a flash photo of a card game during a newspaper gambling exposé; he declined. Gambling was ubiquitous and public gambling houses ran wide open.

segments.title: Neighborhood bars that doubled as dance halls
segments.summary: They compare places like Lutton's with a bar in front and hall behind, their acoustics, and similar spots in Algiers and Marrero.

segments.title: The kitty, and Nick Gagliano's family anniversary party
segments.summary: Bands kept kitties for tips. He describes attorney Nick Gagliano, manager of the George Lewis band, and the Gagliano relatives in medical school.

segments.title: The Gagliano anniversary party with the George Lewis band
segments.summary: A big family party at a Jefferson Parish club with the band playing for hours, a broadcast to make, and Slow Drag tying his bass to a car.

segments.title: Other parties, dances and requests to the band
segments.summary: Organizations gave dances with bands; musicians played what they wanted with some requests, and feeding the kitty bought a request. Reel two begins.

segments.title: Going in with the band; being hassled by club owners
segments.summary: He was always welcomed when entering with a band. The interviewer recalls Bourbon Street and Lutcher's owners hassling him for talking to musicians.

segments.title: Brass bands heard; Eureka drummer Edmund Washington
segments.summary: He heard the Eureka and Young Tuxedo bands. Eureka snare drummer Edmund Washington, a medical school coworker, tipped him off to parades; they discuss the term 'trambone'.

segments.chapter: Dixieland, revival bands and record collectors
segments.title: Hearing the Yerba Buena Jazz Band at the Dawn Club
segments.summary: He defines Dixieland, then recounts the first live band that thrilled him: Lu Watters' Yerba Buena band in San Francisco in late 1946, with red beans and rice and Turk Murphy.

segments.chapter: Dixieland, revival bands and record collectors
segments.title: New Orleans Record Shop and collectors who dismissed Black bands
segments.summary: Collectors around the record shop; one leading collector said George Lewis and Paul Barbarin played Creole music, not jazz.

segments.chapter: Dixieland, revival bands and record collectors
segments.title: Claims of inventing jazz and readers versus improvisers
segments.summary: Nick LaRocca and bayou musicians claimed to have invented jazz; Kid Sheik on Manuel Perez, and the meaning of 'musician' as a reader.

segments.chapter: Dixieland, revival bands and record collectors
segments.title: Jim Crow attitudes and Johnny Bayersdorffer's band
segments.summary: Segregation shaped what people listened to; the interviewer made collectors hear Bayersdorffer's band, whose two best sides he still prizes.

segments.title: Hack bands, Sharkey, and the bind of playing for audiences
segments.summary: Local hack bands could play exceptional jazz; musicians fall into ruts on Bourbon Street, caught between enthusiasts and the public and between critics and observation.

segments.title: Applause after every solo and band form
segments.summary: A solo pianist responded to appreciative crowds. They complain about applause after every solo and discuss form, with Dixieland bands using solo-after-solo formats.

segments.title: Lazy musicians, long breaks and stale bands
segments.summary: Asked about lazy musicians, he says not really; owners wanted long breaks, and full-time bands got stale compared with part-time ones.

segments.title: Fancy drill by social club marching units
segments.summary: The Olympians' paramilitary unit and Odd Fellows' men's and ladies' drill teams in his photographs, and how drill teams get confused.

segments.title: Parade stops at bars and homes; sandwiches in the umbrella
segments.summary: Parades stopped at bars and homes while bands played outside; the interviewer recalls Herman Sherman teaching him to hide sandwiches in an umbrella.

segments.title: Respectable society and jazz; Doc Souchon and others
segments.summary: Nice people and jazz: Doc Souchon as an independent thinker, his father's paintings, Ed Maugham liking barrelhouse, and people sneaking to the Red Light District.

segments.title: Johnny Wiggs, Mahogany Hall wallpaper and Bellocq's book
segments.summary: Wiggs's remarks on disinfecting Mahogany Hall wallpaper; he and Greenwood got quantities of it, and Thurman Reeves brought relics from the building.
